pr_title: Properly initialize string vector when reading large JSON arrays of strings
pr_body:
Fixes #6432 (I assume it fixes #6359, too, because the issue sounds similar, but we don't have the input file).

I've also added support for `.jsonl` replacement scans and a cardinality estimator for reading JSON files (it's VERY crude, but better than nothing - it can be improved in the future).
pr_comments: I'll add a comment explaining why I chose these numbers
I've fixed #6443 in this PR as well

issue_context.title: unexpected exit on read_json_auto()
issue_context.body:
### What happens?

Cli crashes when loading very big json files. I'm not sure what's the supported size limits for loading json files, so this could be also a feature request.

### To Reproduce

Test 1:

```
wget -O test.json "https://www.kartenliebe.de/web-api/calendar-data"
ls -lisah test.json
# 2753933 1,3M -rw-rw-r-- 1 tb tb 1,3M Feb 22 21:53 test.json
./duckdb
# v0.7.1-dev318 c4dc292659
# Enter ".help" for usage hints.
# Connected to a transient in-memory database.
# Use ".open FILENAME" to reopen on a persistent database.
select * from read_json_auto('test.json');
# malloc_consolidate(): invalid chunk size
# Aborted
echo $?
# 134
```

Test 2:

```
wget -O test2.json "https://www.kartenliebe.de/web-api/card-data?occasion=kommunion&themeId=2813&card=fotostreifen-90x210"
ls -lisah test2.json
# 2758495 1,3M -rw-rw-r-- 1 tb tb 1,3M Feb 22 21:58 test2.json
./duckdb
# v0.7.1-dev318 c4dc292659
# Enter ".help" for usage hints.
# Connected to a transient in-memory database.
# Use ".open FILENAME" to reopen on a persistent database.
select * from read_json_auto('test2.json');
# Segmentation fault
echo $?
# 139
```

### OS:

x64 amd

### DuckDB Version:

v0.7.1-dev318 c4dc292659

### DuckDB Client:

cli

### Full Name:

Thomas Bley

### Affiliation:

myself

### Have you tried this on the latest `master` branch?

- [X] I agree

### Have you tried the steps to reproduce? Do they include all relevant data and configuration? Does the issue you report still appear there?

- [X] I agree

I have pushed a fix in #6437

review_comments: Are these real magic numbers, or just here for the joke?

The CSV reader has a witty comment if it has to guess the number of rows in a CSV file without knowing the file size, which also defaults to 42. As for the the other estimate, I've estimated the average size of a JSON object to be 420 bytes mostly because it's 42 * 10, but also because the size of a JSON row in the `lineitem` table is pretty similar at an average of ~360 bytes.

This is obviously not a great estimate, but it's better than estimating nothing because that will default to an estimated cardinality of 0.
Maybe we can do the number of columns * 42 instead? Or are the number of columns not known yet at this stage?

They are known at this time if this is `read_(nd)json(_auto)`, but in JSON you can have one top-level column which is deeply nested, so there's really no guarantees to the size of column. Users may also specify that a deeply nested column should not be unnested by specifying it to be type `JSON`, which means that this column is huge. I can try to make the heuristic slightly smarter but it will be off by a lot in many cases. The best way to do this is to measure the size of the first JSON, which we could do when auto-detecting, but not when columns are manually specified.
